title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents

paper.title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO , a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/KnowGPO .

Right: KnowGPO abstracts heterogeneous states into knowledge states ( 𝐬 i , t \mathbf{s}_{i,t} ) and computes step-level advantages from incremental knowledge gains ( r i , t r_{i,t} ). 1 Introduction LLM-based deep search agents have become a powerful paradigm for knowledge-intensive problem solving, coordinating multi-turn search, evidence inspection, query reformulation, and termination decisions through language-model reasoning ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Unlike conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which typically follows a one-pass retrieve-then-read pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2021 ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) , deep search agents iteratively formulate queries, inspect evidence, update beliefs, and decide when to stop ( Nakano et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2025c ) . This makes deep search a long-horizon sequential decision problem, where success depends on adaptive decisions about what to search, what evidence to keep, and when to terminate . Because supervised fine-tuning mainly imitates surface behavior ( Nakano et al., 2021 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) and cannot optimize such strategic decisions, reinforcement learning has become central to training competitive deep search agents ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ) . However, applying reinforcement learning to deep search agents encounters three coupled difficulties in credit assignment (Figure 1 ). First, terminal outcome rewards used by group-relative methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025 ) are uniformly broadcast to every action, so a single final reward cannot reveal which intermediate decisions were useful, redundant, or harmful. Second, recent process-supervision methods such as GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) that align trajectories by their intermediate states require state recurrence across trajectories, yet deep search rollouts seldom revisit the same observable state even when they acquire the same evidence. Third, dense process rewards derived from changes in the model’s predicted answer probability, as in IGPO ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , or from learned critics and rubric-based reward models ( Shi et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , provide denser signals but are driven by model-internal beliefs or learned proxies rather than by externally verified knowledge. Deep search trajectories vary widely at the level of queries, pages, and reasoning traces, but converge on the same underlying quantity: the task-relevant knowledge they have accumulated toward the correct answer. This knowledge, not observations or model confidence, provides the natural signal for credit assignment in long-horizon search. We propose Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization (KnowGPO) , a RL framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, we decompose the information required to derive the correct answer into a set of atomic knowledge conditions. At every step of a trajectory, we represent its state by the subset of conditions it has satisfied, called its knowledge state . We further define incremental knowledge gain , the increase in satisfied conditions between consecutive steps, as a process reward that scores each action’s immediate contribution. While knowledge-state grouping ensures only semantically comparable steps are contrasted, incremental gain provides the dense signal within each group, enabling fine-grained credit assignment without a learned critic. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, yielding step-level advantages that combine with episode-level outcome advantages through a single mixing coefficient. The result is fine-grained credit assignment for long-horizon deep search without observation matching, without dependence on the model’s own confidence, and without a learned reward model. We train Qwen3-8B with KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks: Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA. KnowGPO improves over outcome-only GRPO by 2.0% to 5.9% and consistently outperforms recent process-supervision baselines including GiGPO and IGPO, with the resulting 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters. In summary, our contributions are threefold: • We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that performs credit assignment in a query-specific knowledge state space rather than over surface observations, enabling within-group comparison across semantically equivalent trajectories. • We introduce incremental knowledge gain as a process reward grounded in the environment, providing dense step-level supervision without observation matching, learned critics, or reliance on model-internal probabilities. • We demonstrate that KnowGPO outperforms outcome-based and recent process-supervision baselines by 3.8% to 4.2% across three deep search benchmarks, with an 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters. 2 Related Work 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for Search Agent Reinforcement learning with verifiable outcome rewards has become the dominant paradigm for post-training deep search agents. Early systems train models to interleave search and reasoning through outcome-based optimization on multi-hop QA ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , showing that group-relative methods such as GRPO scale to multi-turn tool use without learned value functions. Subsequent work scales this paradigm along two axes: harder data through knowledge graphs, web exploration, and synthetic multi-hop generation ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Du et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Chu et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026e ; Team et al., 2026d ) , and refined reward shaping and policy gradient stability for long-horizon rollouts ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, the supervisory signal in most systems remains a binary reward at the end of each trajectory, leaving the contribution of search decisions inside long rollouts unidentified. 2.2 Credit Assignment for Search Agents A growing line of work aims to address long-horizon credit assignment through process-level supervision. GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) extends GRPO with anchor-state grouping, computing step-level advantages by matching trajectories that revisit the same environment state; this mechanism requires reliable state recurrence, which is rare in deep search where retrieved contents and reasoning histories are open-ended. IGPO ( Wang et al., 2026 ) instead derives dense step rewards from the model’s own probability of producing the correct answer, sidestepping state matching but anchoring the signal to internal confidence that can be biased by long, noisy retrieved contexts. A parallel direction introduces externally grounded supervision through learned reward models or rubric decompositions ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) , providing denser feedback than outcome rewards but relying on learned proxies whose calibration is itself a research question, and without producing step groupings that make semantically equivalent decisions directly comparable across trajectories. KnowGPO instead anchors credit assignment to an externally verifiable representation of progress, the set of satisfied atomic knowledge conditions, and uses this representation as both the grouping criterion for within-group comparison and the basis of a process reward grounded in the environment. 3 Method 3.1 Problem Formulation We formulate deep search as a multi-turn sequential decision process. Given a query Q Q and a reference answer y ∗ y^{*} , an agent interacts with a retrieval environment over time steps t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} . At each step the agent produces a reasoning trace and an action a t ∈ { search , answer } a_{t}\in\{\texttt{search},\texttt{answer}\} from its policy π θ ( ⋅ ∣ h t , Q ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},Q) , where h t = ( a 1 , o 1 , … , a t − 1 , o t − 1 ) h_{t}=(a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) is the interaction history and o t o_{t} is the observation returned by the environment (e.g., retrieved documents for search , or a terminal signal for answer ).
